title: Classical music's enduring allure
gist: Elisabeth Braw argues from the Proms and Verbier that classical music festivals are in a supply boom — dozens of new events from Tongyeong to Guadeloupe, many launched in the past three decades — driven by younger audiences and holidaymakers seeking sustained meaningful activity away from overtouristed destinations, with the main risk being managers overexposing the strong incoming generation of musicians.

insights.claim: Classical music festivals have proliferated far beyond the historic Salzburg and Bayreuth core, with dozens of new European festivals plus South Korea's Tongyeong International Music Festival, Ireland's West Cork Chamber Music Festival, Austria's Grafenegg, Turkey's Gümüşlük, Wimbledon's International Music Festival and Guadeloupe's Festival International de Musique Saint-Georges.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Supply expansion on this scale implies real demand growth in live classical, and a competitive market for artist bookings and destination positioning.
insights.locator: The Verbier Festival is part of a remarkable trend

insights.claim: The Verbier Festival, founded 32 years ago, converted a Swiss Alpine town known mostly for skiing into a destination known as much for classical music.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: A cultural anchor can diversify a single-season resort economy into year-round demand — the model other alpine and coastal destinations can copy.
insights.locator: A few days later, I travelled to Verbier

insights.claim: The East German government launched the Dresdner Musikfestspiele in the late 1970s after realising classical music could bring visitors into the country, and the festival still operates.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Culture deployed as a deliberate inbound-tourism and soft-power instrument, with a fifty-year payoff horizon.
insights.locator: In the late 1970s, the East German government

insights.claim: Braw argues classical music is becoming more popular especially among younger people, against the habitual fears that the art form will decline.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: If the demographic claim holds, the consensus decline narrative around classical institutions is mispriced.
insights.quote: Despite the habitual fears that classical music will decline
insights.locator: One could interpret that as a sign of the times

insights.claim: The stated demand driver is that people like being able to spend their holidays pursuing a sustained and meaningful activity rather than passive tourism.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Experiential, skill-adjacent travel as a distinct and growing category — relevant to how premium leisure spend is allocated.
insights.quote: they also like the fact that they can spend their holidays pursuing a sustained and meaningful activity
insights.locator: People, it turns out, like the music

insights.claim: Festivals offer intellectually stimulating experiences far from the suffocating crowds swarming tourist destinations, positioning them as a direct substitute for overtouristed itineraries.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Overtourism backlash is a tailwind for high-price, low-density cultural destinations.
insights.quote: far from the suffocating crowds swarming tourist destinations

insights.claim: The festival product is dense rather than single-event: masterclasses, open rehearsals and several concerts each day, which is what the author identifies as the reason for their popularity.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Programming depth, not star billing alone, is the retention mechanism that brings audiences back annually.
insights.locator: There are masterclasses, open rehearsals and concerts

insights.claim: The generation of musicians now debuting looks likely in time to become even more impressive than the current stars, despite there being quite a few not-so-great ones too.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: A supply-side argument that the artistic quality ceiling is still rising, which supports long-run demand for live performance.

insights.claim: At Verbier, the 15-to-18-year-olds of the Junior Orchestra outshone the soloists in a performance of Carl Orff's Carmina Burana.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence for the pipeline claim, and a reason festivals invest in academy programmes as a talent moat.
insights.locator: As happens every year, the stars were joined

insights.claim: Braw flags the risk that managers and promoters succumb to the temptation of overexposing young musicians at an early age.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Career burn rate is the main threat to the talent pipeline that underpins the sector's growth case.
insights.quote: One can only hope that managers and promoters don’t succumb to the temptation of overexposing them at an early age.

insights.claim: This year's Verbier lineup included Evgeny Kissin, Mischa Maisky, Martha Argerich, Renée Fleming, Esa-Pekka Salonen, Alexandre Kantorow, Yunchan Lim, Bruce Liu, Gianandrea Noseda and Simon Rattle.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Shows how much top-tier talent a 32-year-old mountain festival can now command relative to legacy institutions.
insights.locator: Among the musicians performing at Verbier

insights.claim: The very first Promenade Concert under Sir Henry Wood at the Queen's Hall in summer 1895 already mixed beloved warhorses with new work, including Wagner's Rienzi overture, an aria from Pagliacci, an orchestral Chopin polonaise and a world premiere of a now-forgotten Adolphe Schloesser march.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: The old-plus-new programming formula treated as a modern audience-development innovation is in fact the original design.
insights.locator: On that first night of what would become known as the Proms

insights.claim: The Proms have run 131 years and survived the destruction of Queen's Hall in the Blitz, relocating to the Royal Albert Hall.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Institutional durability across physical destruction — the franchise, not the venue, carries the value.
insights.locator: One hundred and thirty-one years later

insights.claim: At the Proms performance attended, the surprise was South African cellist Abel Selaocoe, who defied convention by singing as well as playing and got the audience to sing along, outshining adequately performed Bach and Beethoven.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Format innovation, not repertoire, is what generated audience response — a signal for how institutions can grow engagement.
insights.locator: Although the Bach and Beethoven were adequately performed
